claims.text: The precursor is based on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and contains 5–10 wt% excess Zr powder as an oxygen getter.
Excess Zr reacts with trace oxygen to form stable ZrO2.
Zr scavenging lowers oxygen chemical potential sufficiently to prevent alpha-HCP nucleation.
TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 decompose sequentially during heating and thereby drive in-situ alloying.
Hydride decomposition releases hydrogen and increases local atomic mobility for diffusion-controlled alloying.
The proposed treatment heats at 10 °C/min to 800 °C, then at 50 °C/min to 1300 °C, followed by an immediate water quench.
An equiatomic five-component alloy has enhanced configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the high-temperature beta-BCC phase of HfNbTaTiZr during rapid cooling.
Rapid quenching bypasses spinodal-decomposition or ordering windows that would otherwise produce alpha-BCC or sigma phases.
Rapid quenching from 1300 °C produces a metastable single-phase beta-BCC HfNbTaTiZr solid solution.
The quenched product reaches greater than 98% relative density.
The quenched product has a grain size of 5–10 µm.
The final oxygen content is below 50 ppm.
The final microstructure is free of alpha-HCP, sigma, and B2 phases.
Removing the Zr getter or using slower cooling produces dual alpha-BCC plus beta-BCC or alpha-HCP structures, larger grains, and higher oxygen content.
Alpha-phase nucleation requires oxygen partial pressure to remain below approximately 10^-10 atm during the TiH2 and ZrH2 decomposition window.
TiH2 decomposes over approximately 500–700 °C under the proposed conditions.
The decomposition temperature of TaH0.5 is less well defined than those of the other listed hydrides.
Alpha-Ti formation is operationally detected by HCP diffraction peaks such as (100) and (002).
The hypothesis is falsified if getter-treated material exhibits alpha-Ti peak intensity above 5% of the primary beta-BCC peak during 500–700 °C or retains less than 90% beta-BCC after quenching.

contradictions.description: The starting blend is described as equiatomic while also containing 5–10 wt% excess Zr. If the mixed-in getter remains in or reacts within the specimen, the resulting alloy is not equiatomic unless Zr loss or getter separation is explicitly accounted for.

Zr powder is mixed into the precursor and is predicted to form ZrO2, yet the final material is called a single-phase beta-BCC solid solution. Retained ZrO2 would constitute an additional phase unless the getter is external or the oxide is removed.
